questions.passage: Oysters were once so plentiful in the Chesapeake Bay that their reefs were a hazard to passing ships. A single adult oyster can filter dozens of gallons of water a day, removing algae and sediment as it feeds. Over-harvesting and disease, however, shrank the population to a small fraction of its historic size. Today, Maryland volunteers grow young oysters in cages hung from their own docks, then move them to protected sanctuary reefs, hoping to restore both the oysters and the clean water they support.
questions.stem: The main idea of this passage is that:
choices: volunteers are helping bring back oysters, which help clean the Bay
disease is the only reason oysters declined
questions.answer_text: volunteers are helping bring back oysters, which help clean the Bay

questions.passage: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery on Maryland’s Eastern Shore around 1822. In 1849 she escaped to Philadelphia, but she did not stay safely in the North. Over the next decade she returned to Maryland about thirteen times, guiding roughly seventy people to freedom along the Underground Railroad. She traveled at night, used songs as coded signals, and later boasted that she “never lost a passenger.” During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a scout and spy.

questions.passage: Before 1952, a trip from Annapolis to Maryland’s Eastern Shore usually meant waiting for a ferry. On busy summer weekends, cars could line up for hours. That changed when the Chesapeake Bay Bridge opened, linking the Western and Eastern Shores by road. The bridge stretches about 4.3 miles over open water. Traffic kept growing, so a second, parallel span opened in 1973. Today millions of drivers cross each year, and many beach towns rely on the visitors the bridge brings.
